Fulfilment writers answer that 'until' marks a limit but does not always imply a reversal in the same terms (compare 2 Samuel 6:23, where Michal had no child 'until' her death). Matthew 23:39 may mean that Jerusalem will see Jesus only when it is forced to acknowledge him at the judgment. And the end of the 'times of the Gentiles' may simply be the end of history at Christ's return.

Future-for-Israel scholars reply that 'Blessed is he who comes' is a greeting of welcome from Psalms 118:26, not a cry of terror, so it fits a repentant Jerusalem better than a judged one. Zechariah 12:10 also pictures Jerusalem looking on the one they pierced and mourning in repentance. Three separate 'until' texts pointing the same way, they argue, form a pattern.
Providence, survival, and the moral warning from Church history

Future-for-Israel writers point out that the Jewish people survived nearly two thousand years of exile, kept their identity, and returned in large numbers to the land, as many prophets foresaw (Isaiah 11:11-12; Ezekiel 36:24). They also warn that the claim that the church has replaced Israel has often been joined in history with contempt for Jews: for example, John Chrysostom's sermons against the Jews (386-387) and Luther's 'On the Jews and Their Lies' (1543). Soulen and Horner argue that supersessionism tends to see Jews as having no further purpose, and that this view made Christian hostility easier. Romans 11:18 warns Gentile branches not to boast against the natural branches.

Fulfilment writers grant the history and condemn it, but argue that a doctrine is judged by Scripture, not by misuse. Many fulfilment theologians have loved and protected Jewish people, and the view itself teaches that Jews are welcome in Christ on equal terms. They also note that Jewish survival and return can be acts of God's providence without being the fulfilment of covenant promises, since the Old Testament ties restoration to repentance (Deuteronomy 30:1-3), while the 1948 state was founded mostly by secular Zionists.

Future-for-Israel scholars reply that they do not claim the fulfilment view causes antisemitism, only that it removes a strong theological guard against it, which Romans 11:28-29 provides. On providence, they argue that God may regather Israel first in unbelief and then bring about repentance, as the order of Ezekiel 36:24-26 and Ezekiel 37:7-10 suggests: gathered, then cleansed; bones joined, then breath.
'Replacement theology' means God has rejected the Jews and Jews can no longer be saved.

No major fulfilment theologian teaches that Jews cannot be saved. Paul, himself a Jew, says God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1-2) and that natural branches can be grafted in again (Romans 11:23). Many Reformed scholars, such as Murray, Vos and Hodge, even expect a future large-scale turning of Jews to Christ.

The fulfilment view holds that Israel's promises are fulfilled in Christ, the true Israel, and shared by all who trust him, Jew and Gentile alike. Most of its defenders reject the label 'replacement' and prefer 'fulfilment' or 'expansion': the believing remnant of Israel was never replaced, and Gentiles were added to Israel's one olive tree (Romans 11:17).
Fulfilment theologians spiritualise everything, so they deny a physical resurrection and a real new earth.

Covenant amillennialists, postmillennialists and progressive covenantalists confess the bodily resurrection and the bodily return of Christ, as the historic creeds do. Hoekema, Riddlebarger and Middleton argue strongly for a renewed, physical creation (Romans 8:19-23; Revelation 21:1-5).

The fulfilment view reads Old Testament promises through their New Testament fulfilment in Christ. It holds that the land promise widens to the whole renewed earth (Romans 4:13; Matthew 5:5), which is a very physical hope. What it denies is a separate future ethnic inheritance of Canaan, not physical fulfilment as such.
Fulfilment theology says God broke his promises to Israel.

Fulfilment writers insist that God kept every promise, citing 2 Corinthians 1:20 and Joshua 21:43-45, which says not one of God's good promises to Israel failed. Their claim is that the promises were kept in a larger way than first expected, not that they were dropped.

On this view God promised a Seed, a land, a throne and a temple, and he gave them in Christ: the Seed is Christ (Galatians 3:16), the throne is at God's right hand (Acts 2:30-36), the temple is Christ and his people (John 2:21; Ephesians 2:21), and the land becomes the world (Romans 4:13). Critics may judge this a reinterpretation, but its holders see it as faithful fulfilment.
Anyone who holds the fulfilment view is antisemitic or anti-Jewish.

A theological claim about how promises are fulfilled is not the same as hostility to a people. Many fulfilment theologians have opposed antisemitism; for example, members of the Confessing Church in Nazi Germany, many of them Reformed or Lutheran, resisted the persecution of Jews. Critics such as Soulen and Horner say supersessionism can make contempt easier, but they do not claim every holder is hostile.

The fulfilment view holds that ethnic Jews are fully welcome in Christ, equal with Gentiles, and are not excluded from salvation. Its careful defenders accept the warning of Romans 11:18-20 against Gentile pride, and they condemn the anti-Jewish writings of Chrysostom and Luther as sin.
Fulfilment theologians simply ignore Romans 11.

Romans 11 is one of the most studied chapters among Reformed and amillennial scholars. There is a whole range of fulfilment readings: Calvin and Wright take 'all Israel' as the whole people of God; Robertson and Merkle take it as all elect Jews through history; Murray, Vos and Hodge expect a future turning of ethnic Israel to Christ.

The fulfilment view takes Romans 11 seriously but reads its promise as salvation through faith in Christ under the new covenant (Romans 11:26-27), not as a restored national kingdom or temple. The disagreement is over what Romans 11 promises, not whether it matters.
Dispensationalists teach two ways of salvation: by law for Israel, by grace for the church.

Some early statements were unclear; a note in the 1909 Scofield Reference Bible on John 1:17 was widely read as contrasting legal obedience and grace as conditions of salvation. But dispensational leaders, including Ryrie and the editors of the New Scofield Reference Bible (1967), clearly reject salvation by works in any age.

Dispensationalists hold that in every age salvation is by grace through faith, based on Christ's death. What changes from one dispensation to another is the content of revelation that faith responds to and the rule of life God gives, not the ground or means of salvation. Ryrie stated this as a central point in 'Dispensationalism'.
Dispensationalists and Christian Zionists support anything the State of Israel does.

Many dispensational scholars say that God's covenant with Israel does not mean approval of every policy of a modern secular government. Some, such as Vlach, separate the theological future of Israel from present political questions. Christian Zionist groups vary widely, and some also support Arab and Palestinian Christians.

Most dispensationalists believe God has a future for ethnic Israel, and many see the 1948 state as at least a setting of the stage for that future. Christian Zionists go further and urge active support for the state, often citing Genesis 12:3. But support for the nation's existence is not the same as endorsing every act of its government, and many holders say so.
Dispensationalism was invented out of nothing in 1830.

Many of its parts are old. Premillennialism goes back to Justin Martyr and Irenaeus in the second century. Hope of a future Jewish conversion was common among Puritans (for example in Thomas Brightman, 1615, and later Increase Mather), and some English and Scottish writers expected a Jewish return to the land long before Darby.

What is new in the 1830s, through John Nelson Darby and the Brethren, is the system: a sharp and lasting distinction between Israel and the church, a pre-tribulation rapture, and dividing history into dispensations in that particular way. It spread through the Niagara Bible Conferences and the Scofield Reference Bible (1909). Both the real roots and the real novelty should be stated.
Dispensationalists think the church is an accident, a 'plan B' God did not intend.

Classic dispensationalists, such as Chafer, Walvoord and Pentecost, called the church age a 'parenthesis' or 'intercalation', but they meant that it was not revealed in the Old Testament, not that God did not plan it. They point to Ephesians 3:5-6, which calls it a mystery hidden in past ages.

Progressive dispensationalists, such as Blaising, Bock and Saucy, drop the 'parenthesis' language. They see the church as the present, inaugurated stage of the one kingdom plan, in which Christ already reigns from David's throne at God's right hand and Jews and Gentiles share the new covenant. Israel's national promises remain for the future stage.
Dispensationalists believe Jews are saved by the Mosaic covenant without Jesus.

Dual-covenant theology, which says Jews can be saved through their own covenant apart from Christ, is held by some liberal theologians and has been charged against a few popular figures. Mainstream dispensationalists strongly reject it. Arnold Fruchtenbaum, a leading dispensational writer, is a Messianic Jew who has spent his life preaching Jesus to Jewish people.

Dispensationalists hold that there is salvation in no other name (Acts 4:12) for Jew or Gentile. They expect Israel's future national salvation to come when Israel looks on the one it pierced (Zechariah 12:10) and believes in Jesus as Messiah (Romans 11:26).
Dispensationalists want war in the Middle East to hasten Armageddon.

Scholarly dispensationalists teach that Christians cannot hasten or fix the date of prophetic events (Acts 1:7), and that believers should pray for peace and do good to all (1 Timothy 2:1-2; Galatians 6:10). Some popular prophecy writing has been sensational, and critics such as Weber and Gorenberg have documented its political influence, but that is not the same as wishing for war.

Dispensationalists believe that a time of great tribulation and a final battle are foretold (Daniel 12:1; Zechariah 14:2-4), and that Christ will end it by his return. Expecting a foretold event is different from trying to cause it.
Does the New Testament have the final word on how Old Testament promises are fulfilled?

This is the main hermeneutical fork. If the New Testament can show a fuller meaning than the Old Testament text alone, promises may be fulfilled in Christ in a larger form; if not, the original sense must still be met.
Yes: the New Testament reveals how the promises are fulfilled, and may show a fuller meaning
No: the New Testament can add to an Old Testament promise but cannot change its original sense
Is Christ himself the true Israel and the one Seed, so that all who belong to him are heirs of Israel's promises?
Galatians 3:16 and 3:29 are central here. If Christ is the true Israel, Israel's identity runs through him to his people; the question is whether a separate national role remains.
Yes, and that settles who Israel is in the promises
Yes, but ethnic Israel still has a special future in God's plan
Are the land promises fulfilled, conditional, or still pending for ethnic Israel?
The land is the hardest test case. Joshua 21:43-45 says the promise was kept; Romans 4:13 widens it to the world; Amos 9:15 and Ezekiel 37:25 speak of a lasting possession.
Fulfilled in Joshua's day and now widened in Christ to the whole renewed earth
Conditional: lost through unfaithfulness, and now taken up into the greater promise in Christ
Still pending: the land belongs to ethnic Israel and will be fully possessed in the future
Does Romans 11:26 promise a future large-scale turning of ethnic Jews to Christ, and if so, what comes with it?
Even many Reformed scholars (Murray, Vos, Hodge) expect a future turning of Jews to Christ. The key question is whether a restored national kingdom in the land comes with it.
A large turning of Jews to Christ, but no restored national kingdom or temple
A turning to Christ that brings Israel's national restoration in the land under the Messiah
Does the thousand-year reign of Revelation 20 come after the second coming of Christ?
If Revelation 19 and 20 are in time order, a future earthly reign follows Christ's return. If Revelation 20 goes back to describe the present age, the millennium is now.
Yes: a future reign on earth follows Christ's return
No: Revelation 20 describes the present age between the two comings
How do you read the present age and the events of AD 70?
Fulfilment views agree that Christ reigns now. They differ over how much prophecy was fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem and how far the gospel will triumph before Christ returns.
AD 70 fulfilled most prophecies of judgment on Israel and ended the old covenant age
The gospel will win most of the nations before Christ returns
Good and evil grow together until Christ returns; the church suffers and witnesses
Is the founding of the State of Israel in 1948 a fulfilment of prophecy?

This separates the future-for-Israel camps. Some see 1948 as direct fulfilment that calls for support; others see a possible setting of the stage; others say the true restoration comes only with Israel's faith in Messiah.
Yes: it fulfils prophecy, and Christians should actively support the state (Genesis 12:3)
It may be a setting of the stage; Israel and the church remain distinct peoples with distinct promises
Not in itself a fulfilment; Israel's restoration comes with faith in Jesus, and Christ already reigns in part now

You read Israel's promises as fulfilled in Christ and shared by his one people, Jew and Gentile, with the millennium as the present reign of Christ. This is the view of Augustine, Calvin, Hoekema, Robertson and Riddlebarger. Progressive covenantalists such as Gentry and Wellum reach similar conclusions on Israel by a different account of the covenants.

You see Christ reigning now and expect the gospel to win most of the nations before he returns. Postmillennialists such as Mathison and Gentry read Israel's promises as fulfilled in Christ, though many, following the Puritans, expect a great conversion of Jews as part of that victory.

You see AD 70 as the great judgment that ended the old covenant age and fulfilled much of the Olivet Discourse and Revelation. Partial preterists such as Gentry and DeMar hold that Israel's promises are fulfilled in Christ and his church, while still expecting Christ's bodily return and final judgment.

You expect a future earthly reign of Christ after his return, while seeing one people of God in Christ. Ladd and Blomberg represent this view; many of its holders expect a future turning of Jews to Christ (Romans 11:26) without a separate program for Israel.

You see Christ already reigning on David's throne and the church as the present stage of the one kingdom plan, while Israel's national promises await fulfilment when Israel turns to Jesus. Blaising, Bock and Saucy represent this view.

You hold that Israel and the church are distinct peoples with distinct promises, and that Israel's national kingdom will come in a future millennium after Christ's return. Darby, Scofield, Walvoord, Ryrie and Pentecost are leading names; many see 1948 as a setting of the stage.

You see the 1948 state as a fulfilment of prophecy and believe Christians should actively support it, often citing Genesis 12:3. Christian Zionism has roots in 19th century British restorationism and today is strong among many evangelical groups; its holders vary on politics.
In Acts 15:16-17, which Old Testament passage does James quote about rebuilding David's fallen tent?

James quotes Amos 9:11-12 to show that Gentiles coming to faith fits the prophets. Fulfilment writers see the rebuilding of David's tent in the church; dispensationalists often see the Gentile mission as a step before Israel's future restoration.
In which year was the Balfour Declaration issued?

Arthur Balfour, the British Foreign Secretary, signed the declaration on 2 November 1917. It supported 'a national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine, while saying the rights of existing non-Jewish communities must not be harmed.
What does Paul stress in Galatians 3:16?
That the law came 430 years after the promise
That the promise was spoken to one 'seed', singular, which is Christ
That Abraham was justified before he was circumcised
That the land is an everlasting possession
Paul notes that the promise speaks of 'seed', not 'seeds', and names that one Seed as Christ. Galatians 3:29 then says all who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed.
Which chapter of Ezekiel contains the vision of the valley of dry bones?
Ezekiel 37:1-14 shows dry bones coming together and then receiving breath, a picture of Israel restored from exile. Some read it of 1948; others read it of spiritual resurrection by the Spirit.
Who wrote 'Der Judenstaat' (The Jewish State) in 1896?
Chaim Weizmann
David Ben-Gurion
Theodor Herzl
Arthur Balfour
Theodor Herzl, an Austro-Hungarian journalist, wrote it in 1896 and organised the First Zionist Congress at Basel in 1897. His Zionism was largely secular and political in aim.
On what date did the United Nations General Assembly vote for the partition of Palestine (Resolution 181)?
29 November 1947
5 June 1967
Resolution 181 was adopted on 29 November 1947. The State of Israel declared its independence on 14 May 1948.
Which passage tells of a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passing between the halves of the animals?

In Genesis 15:17 only God's presence passes between the pieces. Dispensationalists see this as proof that the land covenant is unconditional; fulfilment writers agree it rests on God and say he keeps it in Christ.
Which Old Testament text gives Israel the titles 'kingdom of priests' and 'holy nation' that 1 Peter 2:9 applies to believers?
Exodus 19:5-6 records these titles at Sinai. Peter gives them to the church, which the fulfilment camp reads as a transfer of Israel's identity to the people of Christ.
Who is usually named as the main early systematiser of dispensationalism in the 1830s?
Lewis Sperry Chafer
Charles Ryrie
John Nelson Darby of the Plymouth Brethren shaped the system in the 1830s. Scofield spread it widely through his Reference Bible (1909); Chafer and Ryrie developed it later.
Which verse says the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable, in the context of Israel?

Romans 11:28-29 says Israel is beloved for the fathers' sake, because God's gifts and calling cannot be revoked. Future-for-Israel scholars rely on this heavily; fulfilment scholars read it of Israel's salvation in Christ.
Which New Testament book calls the first covenant 'obsolete' and 'ready to vanish away' after quoting Jeremiah 31?
Romans
Galatians
Hebrews
Hebrews 8:8-12 quotes the new covenant from Jeremiah 31:31-34, and Hebrews 8:13 draws the conclusion. Fulfilment writers use this against a future return to temple sacrifices.
In what year did the Roman army under Titus destroy the Jerusalem temple?
AD 33
AD 135
The temple was burned in AD 70 after a long siege, as Josephus records in 'The Jewish War'. The war began in AD 66; the Bar Kokhba revolt was crushed in AD 135.

The fulfilment case begins with the apostles' own words: every promise of God has found its 'Yes' in Jesus (2 Corinthians 1:20), and the promise to Abraham was made to his seed, 'who is Christ' (Galatians 3:16). Jesus relives Israel's story, from Egypt to the wilderness to the mountain, and succeeds where the nation failed, so that he is the true Israel, the true vine and the true temple (Matthew 2:15; John 15:1; John 2:21). The New Testament then applies Israel's titles, covenant and hope to all who are in him: believing Gentiles are Abraham's seed (Galatians 3:29), a royal priesthood and holy nation (1 Peter 2:9), and members of the commonwealth of Israel (Ephesians 2:12, 19). Abraham himself looked beyond Canaan to a heavenly country, and Paul says he was promised the world (Hebrews 11:16; Romans 4:13), which is why the meek inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). Peter preached that the risen Christ already sits on David's throne (Acts 2:30-36), and James saw David's fallen tent rebuilt as Gentiles turned to God (Acts 15:16-17). Hebrews calls the old order a shadow now obsolete (Hebrews 8:13), so a return to an earthly temple and land program would be a step backwards. On this reading nothing God promised has failed; it has all been kept, and kept more gloriously than Israel first imagined, in Christ and his one people.

The future case begins with the character of God: he swore by himself to Abraham (Hebrews 6:13), cut the covenant alone (Genesis 15:17-18), and tied Israel's survival as a nation to the fixed order of the sun and moon (Jeremiah 31:35-37). Promises given to a specific people about a specific land, with specific borders, cannot be fully kept by giving something else to someone else, however glorious. Paul, writing after the cross, still says that to his unbelieving kinsmen belong 'the covenants' and 'the promises' (Romans 9:4), that they are beloved for the fathers' sake, and that God's calling of them is irrevocable (Romans 11:28-29). The apostles asked the risen Jesus when, not whether, he would restore the kingdom to Israel, and he corrected only their timing (Acts 1:6-7); Peter later spoke of a coming 'restoration of all things' spoken by the prophets (Acts 3:21). Jesus promised the twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes 'in the regeneration' (Matthew 19:28) and told Jerusalem it would see him again when it welcomed him (Matthew 23:39). The New Testament adds Gentiles to Israel's blessings, as the prophets foretold (Isaiah 19:24-25), without cancelling Israel's own inheritance. On this reading, God's faithfulness to Israel is the guarantee of his faithfulness to the church.
